title: How One San Diego Neighborhood Broke a 10-Year Streak of Hate Crimes
summary: Hillcrest, San Diego’s LGBTQ+ neighborhood, saw hate crimes drop for the first time since 2016 after Flock cameras helped police generate leads and act.
body_markdown:
- Over the past decade, Hillcrest recorded more hate crimes than any other San Diego neighborhood.
- Since Flock was introduced, hate crimes have dropped for the first time since 2016.
- The impact extends beyond Hillcrest. In Ellisville, Missouri, Flock helped investigators identify a vehicle connected to an alleged hate-motivated attack.
- Hillcrest residents, workers, and business owners are calling for continued Flock support.
- We introduced robust, industry-leading safeguards in August to support this progress.


‍


## **A decade of hate-fuelled violence. Then, a turning point.**


For ten years, one neighborhood carried the heaviest burden of hate-driven crime. That is changing.


Hillcrest has long been the heart of San Diego’s LGBTQ+ community. It has also recorded more hate crimes than any other neighborhood in the city.


A man who has worked at gay bars and clubs in Hillcrest for decades watched the attacks escalate. In May 2024, he was struck in the eye by a pellet gun. He thought he and his two coworkers had been hit by real bullets and were going to die. He survived, but his eye is permanently damaged, and he lives with PTSD.


The people responsible were never caught. “The intent and the violence and the trauma are still there,” he said.


## **What changed in Hillcrest.**


In July 2024, Flock cameras went up at 14 locations in Hillcrest ahead of Pride. When pellet gun shooters returned to local clubs that September, the cameras captured their car.


Now the numbers have turned.


Hate crimes in Hillcrest have dropped for the first time since 2016.


## **What investigators say.**


The lieutenant who oversees SDPD’s hate crime unit described the difference: “All of the incidents prior to the ALPR cameras being installed had gone unsolved. Immediately after the cameras go up, that’s when we start generating leads, and we’re able to actually act on something.”


A Hillcrest nightclub owner said the cameras act as a deterrent, because people who want to commit crimes know there’s no way around getting caught.


## **Stopping hate beyond Hillcrest.**


Hillcrest isn’t the only place where this kind of support matters. In Ellisville, Missouri, police say a man was lured to a park through a dating app and beaten by a group hiding in the bushes. Police believe there may be other attacks that were never reported.


Flock cameras helped investigators identify a vehicle connected to the case, and charges were filed the next day.


## **Our safeguards and commitment to community safety.**


This August, we introduced industry-leading safeguards because no community should have to live in fear of being targeted by people who want to do harm and get away with it.


Flock is designed for local governance. We welcome local regulations, as communities like San Francisco have introduced, that let us continue to serve the progress seen in Hillcrest.


Progress happens when communities have access to the tools that keep them safe. We hope to serve the Hillcrest community again soon.
